items.title: Dolly Parton — 5 clips (watermark top-right, doppio background, stroke+shadow)
items.style: One scene per provided clip, in the given order. Stay strictly grounded on each clip transcript; do not invent facts. Each scene is a single sentence or two, punchy, quickly paced, about 40 words per scene.

source.source_text: A five-clip teaser of Dolly Parton's best moments, drawn from four interviews (WIRED, 60 Minutes Australia, Dan Rather at Dollywood, Conan).

segments.topic: WIRED introduction and her soprano register
segments.source_text: Dolly introduces the WIRED autocomplete interview and jokes about her voice, explaining that she is a soprano.

segments.topic: The Dollywood empire — millions and its roller coasters
segments.source_text: Inside Dollywood: how Dolly turned her hometown dream into a 300-million-dollar theme park and keeps building roller coasters.

segments.topic: Whitney Houston's cover of 'I Will Always Love You'
segments.source_text: When Whitney Houston cut Dolly's song, the world went platinum and Dolly, who kept the publishing, understood the lifelong value of owning her rights.

segments.topic: The bronze statue and the line about pigeons
segments.source_text: Dolly's hometown erected a bronze statue for her — and her father's line kept her modest: 'To pigeons you're just another outdoor restroom.'

output.text:
Dolly Parton kicks off the Wired autocomplete interview by joking about her voice. She addresses the audience and playfully explains that she is a soprano. This description immediately sets a high expectation for the musical talent being discussed. Her response to the question about her vocal range highlights her unique singing ability. Dolly clarifies that being a soprano means possessing a very high singing quality, indicating she is a very high singer. This insight into her voice positions Dolly Parton as an exceptional vocalist in the world of music. The reference to being a soprano emphasizes the high and clear nature of

Dolly breaks down what made Jolene a global hit: the shared vulnerability in wanting and fearing to lose someone. Every man feels this deep-seated fear that someone more attractive could steal what he loves. This universal anxiety drives the song's appeal because everyone experiences that feeling of being vulnerable. Jolene herself embodies this fragility, openly admitting that other girls are prettier, which fuels the tension in the relationship. This vulnerability makes her experience relatable to anyone who has ever felt insecure about their place in love. The song taps into this shared human experience

And Parton is constantly pushing forward with her Dollywood empire, which has grown into a massive theme park drawing nearly four million visitors last year. This incredible venture includes a $300 million program focused on expanding the park and building a new resort slated to open next summer. She continues to add exciting entertainment, like the new fire chaser Express roller coaster, demonstrating her relentless drive.

When Whitney Houston recorded Dolly Parton's song, it caused a massive global sensation and brought immense financial rewards. Dolly Parton, by retaining ownership of her publishing rights, truly grasped the lasting worth of securing those assets. The recording of this song propelled it to worldwide success, making it a monumental hit across the globe. This event underscored the significant financial implications of owning intellectual property in the music industry. Dolly Parton maintained control over her publishing, which ensured she understood the enduring and lifelong value of those rights. This ownership provided her with a lasting benefit from

Dolly Parton's hometown honored her with a bronze statue erected in the courthouse yard. Her father offered a humble perspective on her fame, reminding everyone that while she was an idol to fans, to the pigeons, she was simply another outdoor restroom. This story highlights the grounded nature of Dolly's upbringing despite her massive global success.
